Physiology-01.question: ১) Only water is transported through
২) Site of blood cell production at developing fetus
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Liver. During fetal life, the liver is the major site of hematopoiesis (blood cell production).

Stages of fetal hematopoiesis:

  1. Yolk sac ✓
    → Earliest site (first few weeks of gestation)

  2. Liver ✓
    → Main site during mid-fetal life

  3. Red bone marrow ✓
    → Becomes the major site in late fetal life and after birth

  4. Thymus ✗
    → Site of T-cell maturation, not blood cell production

High-yield Hematology recall:

Age Main site of hematopoiesis
Early embryo Yolk sac
Fetal period (major) Liver
Late fetus & after birth Red bone marrow

Exam pearl:
Fetal hematopoiesis sequence: Yolk sac → Liver → Bone marrow.

Physiology-01.question: ৩) Movement of chromosome during cell division
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Microtubule. Microtubules form the mitotic spindle, which attaches to chromosomes and helps their movement during cell division.

Functions:

  • Microtubule ✓
    → Forms spindle fibres
    → Moves chromosomes during mitosis and meiosis

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Ribosome ✗
    → Responsible for protein synthesis.

  • Centrosome ✗
    → Organizes microtubules and forms spindle poles but does not directly move chromosomes.

  • Proteasome ✗
    → Degrades unwanted proteins.

High-yield Cell biology recall:

Structure Function
Microtubules Chromosome movement during cell division
Centrosome Spindle organization
Ribosome Protein synthesis
Proteasome Protein degradation

Exam pearl:
Spindle fibres (microtubules) pull chromosomes to opposite poles during mitosis.

Physiology-01.question: ৪) Sky rise of ESR is found in
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Giant cell arteritis. A “sky-high” or very markedly elevated ESR is classically seen in giant cell arteritis due to intense inflammation and increased acute-phase proteins.

ESR changes:

  • Giant cell arteritis ✓
    → Very high ESR (often >100 mm/hr)
    → Increased fibrinogen causes rouleaux formation

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Polycythaemia vera ✗
    → Increased RBC mass increases blood viscosity → ESR is low

  • Pregnancy ✗
    → ESR may be mildly increased due to increased fibrinogen, but not usually “sky-high”

  • MI ✗
    → ESR may rise after myocardial infarction but usually not extreme

High-yield ESR recall:

Condition ESR
Giant cell arteritis Markedly ↑↑ (“sky-high”)
Rheumatoid arthritis ↑
Pregnancy Mild ↑
Polycythaemia vera ↓

Exam pearl:
Sky-high ESR → think giant cell arteritis, temporal arteritis, severe inflammation.

Physiology-01.question: ৫) Protein involved in gap junction
৬) Amount of formed element in blood
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is 45%. Formed elements (RBCs, WBCs, and platelets) make up approximately 45% of total blood volume, which is called the haematocrit.

Composition of blood:

  • Formed elements ✓ → ~45%

    • RBCs (majority)

    • WBCs

    • Platelets

  • Plasma → ~55%

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 30% ✗ → Too low for normal blood cell volume.

  • 70% ✗ → Incorrect; plasma is not this high.

  • 55% ✗ → Represents plasma portion.

High-yield Hematology recall:

Component Percentage
Formed elements ~45%
Plasma ~55%

Exam pearl:
Blood = Plasma (55%) + Formed elements (45%).

Physiology-01.question: ৭) Basic substances of protoplasm exclude
৮) Mononuclear leukocyte
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Monocyte. Monocytes are mononuclear leukocytes because they contain a single, non-lobed nucleus.

Classification of leukocytes:

  • Mononuclear leukocytes ✓
    → Monocyte, lymphocyte

  • Polymorphonuclear leukocytes (granulocytes)
    → Neutrophil, eosinophil, basophil
    → Have multilobed nuclei

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Neutrophil ✗ → Polymorphonuclear leukocyte

  • Eosinophil ✗ → Polymorphonuclear leukocyte

  • Basophil ✗ → Polymorphonuclear leukocyte

High-yield Hematology recall:

Type Cells
Mononuclear Monocyte, lymphocyte
Polymorphonuclear Neutrophil, eosinophil, basophil

Exam pearl:
Mono + nucleus = Monocyte and lymphocyte.

Physiology-01.question: ৯) Most prevalent plasma protein
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Albumin. Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein, contributing about 60% of total plasma proteins.

Functions of albumin:

  • Maintains plasma colloid osmotic pressure

  • Transports substances (fatty acids, hormones, drugs)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Globulin ✗
    → Second most abundant plasma protein; includes antibodies and transport proteins.

  • Fibrinogen ✗
    → Important for blood coagulation but present in a much smaller amount.

  • Prothrombin ✗
    → Clotting factor present in very small concentration.

High-yield Hematology recall:

Plasma protein Main function
Albumin (most abundant) Maintains oncotic pressure
Globulin Immunity & transport
Fibrinogen Clot formation
Prothrombin Coagulation factor

Exam pearl:
Most abundant plasma protein = Albumin (~4 g/dL; ~60% of plasma proteins).

Physiology-01.question: ১০) Maximum components of cell membrane
১১) Site of synthesis ofganmma globulin
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Plasma cell. Gamma globulins are immunoglobulins (antibodies) synthesized and secreted mainly by plasma cells, which are differentiated B lymphocytes.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Liver ✗
    → Synthesizes many plasma proteins, especially albumin and clotting factors, not gamma globulins.

  • Spleen ✗
    → Important lymphoid organ involved in immune responses but not the main site of antibody synthesis.

  • Bone marrow ✗
    → Produces B-cell precursors and contains plasma cells, but the antibody-secreting cells are plasma cells.

High-yield Immunology recall:

Substance Source
Gamma globulin (Immunoglobulin) Plasma cells
Albumin Liver
Fibrinogen Liver
Antibody production Activated B cells → Plasma cells

Exam pearl:
Plasma cell = antibody factory → produces gamma globulins.

Physiology-01.question: ১২) Stuart factor
১৩) Cytoskeleton excludes
১৪) Cell membrane is semipermeable because of having
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Lipid. The lipid bilayer of the cell membrane makes it selectively (semi-) permeable by allowing lipid-soluble substances to pass while restricting many water-soluble molecules.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Protein ✗
    → Provides transport channels, carriers, and receptors, but is not the main basis of semipermeability.

  • Carbohydrate ✗
    → Mainly involved in cell recognition (glycoproteins/glycolipids).

  • Glycolipid ✗
    → Important for cell recognition and membrane stability.

High-yield Cell membrane recall:

Component Main function
Phospholipid bilayer Selective permeability barrier
Protein Transport & receptors
Cholesterol Membrane stability
Glycolipid Cell recognition

Exam pearl:
Cell membrane semipermeability is mainly due to the phospholipid bilayer.

Physiology-01.question: ১৫) Responsible for decoding genetic message
১৬) Plasma protein is increased in
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Multiple myeloma. Plasma proteins, especially gamma globulins (immunoglobulins), are increased due to excessive production of monoclonal immunoglobulin by malignant plasma cells.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Malaria ✗
    → May cause anaemia and altered immune response but not typically increased plasma proteins.

  • Nephrotic syndrome ✗
    → Causes loss of plasma proteins (especially albumin) in urine → ↓ plasma protein.

  • Prematurity ✗
    → Associated with low immunoglobulin levels due to immature immune system.

High-yield Plasma protein recall:

Condition Plasma protein change
Multiple myeloma ↑ Gamma globulin (M protein)
Nephrotic syndrome ↓ Albumin
Liver failure ↓ Albumin & clotting proteins
Chronic inflammation ↑ Globulins

Exam pearl:
Multiple myeloma → malignant plasma cells → excess immunoglobulin → increased plasma protein.

Physiology-01.question: ১৭) Membrane transport system with downhill electrochemical gradient
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Facilitated diffusion. It is a passive transport mechanism where substances move down their electrochemical gradient through specific membrane proteins without using energy (ATP).

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Primary active transport ✗
    → Moves substances against the electrochemical gradient using ATP (e.g., Na⁺/K⁺ pump).

  • Co-transport ✗
    → Secondary active transport; uses the energy stored in another ion gradient (e.g., Na⁺-glucose cotransporter).

  • Counter transport ✗
    → Secondary active transport where substances move in opposite directions (e.g., Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger).

High-yield Physiology recall:

Transport type Gradient Energy
Facilitated diffusion Downhill electrochemical gradient No ATP
Primary active transport Against gradient ATP
Co-transport Against gradient using ion gradient Indirect energy
Counter transport Against gradient using ion gradient Indirect energy

Exam pearl:
Downhill movement = passive transport → facilitated diffusion.

Physiology-01.question: ১৮) Serum is plasma devoid of
১৯) Erythropoietin is secreted from
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Kidney. Erythropoietin (EPO) is mainly secreted by peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney in response to hypoxia.

Functions:

  • Stimulates red bone marrow to increase RBC production (erythropoiesis)

  • Maintains normal red cell mass

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Liver ✗
    → Produces erythropoietin mainly during fetal life.

  • Lung ✗
    → Not a source of EPO.

  • Bone marrow ✗
    → Site of RBC production, not EPO secretion.

High-yield Hematology recall:

Substance Source
Erythropoietin Kidney (adult)
Erythropoiesis Red bone marrow
Main stimulus Hypoxia

Exam pearl:
Adult: Kidney makes EPO → Bone marrow makes RBCs.

Physiology-01.question: ২০) Integral protein of RBC membrane
Physiology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Anion exchange protein. The major integral membrane protein of RBCs is Band 3 protein (anion exchanger), which transports chloride and bicarbonate ions across the RBC membrane.

RBC membrane proteins:

  • Anion exchange protein (Band 3) ✓
    → Integral membrane protein
    → Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ exchange (chloride shift)

  • Ankyrin ✗
    → Peripheral membrane protein; connects spectrin cytoskeleton to Band 3

  • Spectrin ✗
    → Peripheral cytoskeletal protein maintaining RBC shape

  • Streptomycin ✗
    → Antibiotic, unrelated

High-yield RBC membrane recall:

Protein Type Function
Band 3 (Anion exchange protein) Integral Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ exchange
Spectrin Peripheral RBC shape & flexibility
Ankyrin Peripheral Links spectrin to Band 3

Exam pearl:
RBC integral membrane protein = Band 3 (anion exchange protein).

Physiology-01.question: ২১) Synthesis of Hb starts from
২২) Haeme containing proteins excludes
Physiology-01.exp:
Haeme-containing proteins possess a haeme prosthetic group, which consists of protoporphyrin IX with a central ferrous iron (Fe²⁺). These proteins are involved in oxygen transport, oxygen storage, electron transport, and enzymatic oxidation-reduction reactions.

Inositol is a carbohydrate (cyclohexanehexol) that functions in cell signalling (e.g., phosphatidylinositol, IP₃ pathway). It is not a protein and does not contain a haeme group.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Haemoglobin — A haeme-containing protein responsible for oxygen transport in blood.

  • C. Myoglobin — A haeme-containing protein that stores oxygen in skeletal and cardiac muscle.

  • D. Cytochrome C — A haeme-containing electron transport protein involved in the mitochondrial electron transport chain.

High-yield Recall

Topic Key Point
Haeme group Protoporphyrin IX + Fe²⁺
Haeme-containing proteins Haemoglobin, Myoglobin, Cytochromes, Catalase, Peroxidase
Function of haemoglobin Oxygen transport
Function of myoglobin Oxygen storage in muscle
Function of cytochrome C Electron transport in mitochondria
Inositol Cell signalling molecule; not a haeme-containing protein
Common MCQ trap Inositol is neither a protein nor a haeme-containing compound

Exam pearl: Haeme-containing proteins include haemoglobin, myoglobin, cytochromes, catalase, and peroxidase; inositol is a signalling molecule and lacks a haeme group.

Physiology-01.question: ২৩) Nucleus occupying whole of the cytoplasm
২৪) Non protein nitrogenous substance in plasma excludes
Physiology-01.exp:
Non-protein nitrogenous (NPN) substances are nitrogen-containing compounds present in plasma that are not part of proteins. They are mainly end-products of protein and nucleic acid metabolism.

Common NPN substances include:

  • Urea

  • Creatinine

  • Creatine

  • Uric acid

  • Ammonia

  • Amino acids

Bilirubin is a bile pigment produced from the breakdown of haeme. It does not contain nitrogen and therefore is not a non-protein nitrogenous substance.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Ammonia — A non-protein nitrogenous compound formed during amino acid metabolism.

  • B. Creatine — A non-protein nitrogenous compound involved in energy storage in muscle.

  • C. Creatinine — A non-protein nitrogenous waste product of creatine metabolism and an important marker of renal function.

High-yield Recall

Topic Key Point
Non-protein nitrogen (NPN) substances Urea, creatinine, creatine, uric acid, ammonia, amino acids
Major NPN constituent Urea
Clinical importance of creatinine Marker of glomerular filtration rate (GFR)
Bilirubin Haeme degradation product; not nitrogenous
Common MCQ trap Bilirubin is non-protein but not a nitrogen-containing compound

Exam pearl: Non-protein nitrogen (NPN) refers to nitrogen-containing plasma compounds other than proteins; bilirubin is excluded because it is a bile pigment, not a nitrogenous substance.

Physiology-01.question: ২৫) Not granulocyte
২৬) Normal Hb
Physiology-01.exp:
Hb A (α₂β₂) is the normal adult haemoglobin, accounting for 95–98% of total haemoglobin in healthy adults. It is responsible for the normal transport of oxygen from the lungs to tissues.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • B. Hb C — An abnormal haemoglobin variant caused by a mutation in the β-globin gene; associated with Hb C disease.

  • C. Hb S — An abnormal haemoglobin due to a β-globin mutation (Glu → Val at position 6); causes sickle cell disease.

  • D. Hb H — An abnormal haemoglobin (β₄ tetramer) seen in α-thalassaemia (Hb H disease).

High-yield Recall

Topic Key Point
Normal adult haemoglobin Hb A (α₂β₂)
Percentage of Hb A 95–98%
Minor adult haemoglobin Hb A₂ (α₂δ₂): 2–3.5%
Fetal haemoglobin Hb F (α₂γ₂): <1% in adults
Hb S Sickle cell disease
Hb C Hb C disease
Hb H β₄ tetramer; α-thalassaemia
Common MCQ trap Hb A is the normal adult Hb; Hb F is the predominant fetal Hb

Exam pearl: Normal adult haemoglobin is Hb A (α₂β₂), which constitutes approximately 95–98% of total haemoglobin in adults.

Physiology-01.question: ২৭) Lysosomes contain -
Physiology-01.exp:
.

Lysosomes are membrane-bound organelles containing acid hydrolases (hydrolytic enzymes) that function optimally at an acidic pH (~5). These enzymes digest intracellular and extracellular materials, including proteins, lipids, carbohydrates, and nucleic acids, playing a key role in intracellular digestion and autophagy.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Hydrophobic enzymes — Incorrect. Lysosomes contain hydrolytic, not hydrophobic, enzymes.

  • C. Pro enzymes — Incorrect. Lysosomal enzymes are active acid hydrolases, not proenzymes.

  • D. Growth hormones — Incorrect. Growth hormone is secreted by the anterior pituitary, not stored in lysosomes.

High-yield Recall

Topic Key Point
Lysosomal enzymes Acid hydrolases (hydrolytic enzymes)
Optimum pH ~5 (acidic)
Main function Intracellular digestion and autophagy
Organelles digested Damaged organelles and macromolecules
Clinical correlation Lysosomal storage diseases (e.g., Tay-Sachs, Gaucher, Niemann-Pick)
Common MCQ trap Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes, not digestive enzymes functioning at neutral pH

Exam pearl: Lysosomes are the cell's "digestive system," containing acid hydrolases that degrade cellular waste and worn-out organelles.

Physiology-01.question: ২৮) Primary clotting factor excludes
Physiology-01.exp:
The primary (plasma) clotting factors are coagulation proteins present in the circulating blood. They include fibrinogen (Factor I), prothrombin (Factor II), and stable factor (Factor VII).

Tissue factor (Factor III) is not a plasma clotting factor. It is a membrane-bound lipoprotein expressed by subendothelial cells and is released after tissue injury to initiate the extrinsic coagulation pathway.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Fibrinogen (Factor I) — A plasma clotting factor converted to fibrin by thrombin.

  • B. Prothrombin (Factor II) — A plasma clotting factor converted to thrombin.

  • D. Stable factor (Factor VII) — A vitamin K-dependent plasma clotting factor involved in the extrinsic pathway.

High-yield Recall

Topic Key Point
Factor I Fibrinogen
Factor II Prothrombin
Factor III Tissue factor (Tissue thromboplastin); not a plasma factor
Factor VII Stable factor; vitamin K-dependent
Extrinsic pathway Tissue factor (III) + Factor VII
Common MCQ trap Factor III is tissue-derived, whereas most coagulation factors circulate in plasma

Exam pearl: Tissue factor (Factor III) is a tissue-derived initiator of the extrinsic pathway, not a circulating plasma clotting factor.

Physiology-01.question: ২৯) Genotype for AB blood group
৩০) The extrinsic pathway is assessed by...
Physiology-01.exp:
Prothrombin Time (PT) assesses the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways.

PT primarily evaluates:

  • Factor VII (extrinsic pathway)

  • Factors X, V, II (prothrombin), and I (fibrinogen) (common pathway)

PT is prolonged in:

  • Factor VII deficiency

  • Vitamin K deficiency

  • Warfarin therapy

  • Liver disease

  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. BT (Bleeding Time) — Assesses platelet function and vascular integrity, not the coagulation pathways.

  • B. CT (Clotting Time) — An outdated, non-specific test that evaluates overall coagulation; not specific for the extrinsic pathway.

  • D. APTT (Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time) — Assesses the intrinsic and common pathways (Factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II, and I).

High-yield Recall

Topic Key Point
Extrinsic pathway test PT (Prothrombin Time)
Intrinsic pathway test APTT
Common pathway factors X, V, II, I
Extrinsic pathway factor VII
BT assesses Platelet function and vascular integrity
PT prolonged in Warfarin therapy, vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, Factor VII deficiency
Common MCQ trap PT = Extrinsic; APTT = Intrinsic

Exam pearl: Remember: "Play Tennis (PT) Outside (Extrinsic), Play Table Tennis (APTT) Inside (Intrinsic)."

Physiology-01.question: ৩১) Membranous organelle
৩২) Key reaction of coagulation in both pathway is
Physiology-01.exp:
The intrinsic and extrinsic coagulation pathways converge at the activation of Factor X (Stuart–Prower factor), making it the key reaction common to both pathways.

  • Extrinsic pathway: Tissue factor (Factor III) + Factor VIIa → Factor X activation

  • Intrinsic pathway: Factors XII → XI → IX + VIII → Factor X activation

Activated Factor Xa, together with Factor Va, calcium, and phospholipids, forms the prothrombinase complex, which converts prothrombin (Factor II) to thrombin.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Activation of Factor VII — Occurs only in the extrinsic pathway.

  • B. Activation of Factor II (Prothrombin) — Occurs after the common pathway begins; it is not the convergence point.

  • C. Activation of Factor XII — Initiates the intrinsic pathway only.

High-yield Recall

Topic Key Point
Common pathway begins at Factor X activation
Extrinsic pathway III + VII → X
Intrinsic pathway XII → XI → IX + VIII → X
Factor Xa function Converts prothrombin (II) to thrombin (IIa)
Final step Thrombin converts fibrinogen (I) to fibrin
Common MCQ trap Factor X is the point where intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converge

Exam pearl: Remember: Both intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converge at the activation of Factor X—the start of the common coagulation pathway.

Physiology-01.question: ৩৩) Bulk transport system
৩৪) Which enzyme is required in fibrinolysis?
Physiology-01.exp:
Fibrinolysis is the process of breaking down fibrin clots after haemostasis.

The key enzyme responsible is plasmin, which is formed by activation of plasminogen by:

  • Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA)

  • Urokinase (uPA)

Plasmin digests fibrin into fibrin degradation products (FDPs), including D-dimer.

Note: Although the option lists plasminogen, the actual enzyme is plasmin. In many undergraduate MCQs, plasminogen is accepted because it is the inactive precursor of plasmin.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • B. Caspases — Enzymes involved in apoptosis, not fibrinolysis.

  • C. Thrombin — Converts fibrinogen to fibrin, promoting clot formation rather than clot breakdown.

  • D. Antithrombin III — Inhibits thrombin and factors IXa, Xa, XIa, XIIa; it is an anticoagulant, not a fibrinolytic enzyme.

High-yield Recall

Topic Key Point
Fibrinolytic enzyme Plasmin
Inactive precursor Plasminogen
Activators of plasminogen tPA, urokinase
Function of plasmin Degrades fibrin clot into FDPs and D-dimer
Thrombin Forms fibrin clot
Antithrombin III Inhibits thrombin and activated clotting factors
Common MCQ trap Plasmin is the enzyme; plasminogen is its inactive precursor

Exam pearl: The enzyme responsible for fibrinolysis is plasmin; plasminogen is its inactive zymogen activated by tPA or urokinase.

Physiology-01.question: ৩৫) Processing, packaging, labelling & delivery of proteins & lipids
৩৬) Intrinsic coagulation pathway starts with
Physiology-01.exp:
The intrinsic coagulation pathway is initiated by the activation of Factor XII (Hageman factor) when blood comes into contact with a negatively charged surface, such as exposed collagen or subendothelial tissue.

The sequence is:

  • Factor XII → XIIa

  • Factor XI → XIa

  • Factor IX → IXa

  • Factor IXa + Factor VIIIa + Ca²⁺ + phospholipid → Factor X activation

  • The pathway then enters the common pathway.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Activation of Factor VII — Initiates the extrinsic pathway.

  • B. Activation of Factor II (Prothrombin) — Occurs in the common pathway, after Factor X activation.

  • D. Activation of Factor X — Marks the beginning of the common pathway, not the intrinsic pathway.

High-yield Recall

Topic Key Point
Intrinsic pathway starts with Factor XII (Hageman factor)
Extrinsic pathway starts with Tissue factor (III) + Factor VII
Common pathway starts with Factor X activation
Intrinsic pathway sequence XII → XI → IX + VIII → X
Test for intrinsic pathway APTT
Common MCQ trap Factor XII initiates the intrinsic pathway, but its deficiency usually does not cause bleeding despite prolonging APTT

Exam pearl: Intrinsic pathway begins with activation of Factor XII; both intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converge at Factor X.

Physiology-01.question: ৩৭) Propagation of action potential through
৩৮) INR in a patient undergoing warfarin therapy -
Physiology-01.exp:
The International Normalized Ratio (INR) is used to monitor warfarin therapy by standardizing the Prothrombin Time (PT).

For most clinical indications (e.g., atrial fibrillation, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism), the target INR is 2.0–3.0. This range provides effective anticoagulation while minimizing the risk of bleeding.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. 1.5–1.8 — Subtherapeutic for most indications; increased risk of thrombosis.

  • B. 0.9–1.3 — Normal INR in individuals not receiving anticoagulants.

  • C. 4.0–5.0 — Supratherapeutic; associated with a significantly increased risk of bleeding.

High-yield Recall

Topic Key Point
Normal INR 0.9–1.2 (approximately 1.0)
Therapeutic INR (most indications) 2.0–3.0
Mechanical mitral valve (high-risk) 2.5–3.5
Drug monitored by INR Warfarin
Coagulation test PT/INR assesses the extrinsic pathway
Common MCQ trap Warfarin is monitored by PT/INR, whereas heparin is monitored by APTT

Exam pearl: Remember: "Warfarin → PT/INR (target 2–3); Heparin → APTT."

Physiology-01.question: ৩৯) Internal environment
৪০) ICF contains large amount of all of the following except
৪১) Agglutinogens are present in
Physiology-01.exp:
Agglutinogens are antigens present on the red blood cell (RBC) membrane. In the ABO blood group system, these are:

  • Antigen A

  • Antigen B

These antigens determine an individual's blood group. When incompatible blood is transfused, the recipient's antibodies (agglutinins) react with these agglutinogens, causing agglutination and haemolysis.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • B. Platelet membrane — Platelets are not the site of ABO agglutinogens in standard physiology.

  • C. Serum — Serum contains agglutinins (antibodies), not agglutinogens.

  • D. WBC membrane — White blood cells do not carry the ABO agglutinogens responsible for blood grouping.

High-yield Recall

Topic Key Point
Agglutinogens Antigens on RBC membrane
Agglutinins Antibodies in plasma/serum
Blood group A A antigen, anti-B antibody
Blood group B B antigen, anti-A antibody
Blood group AB A & B antigens, no anti-A/anti-B antibodies
Blood group O No A/B antigens, both anti-A & anti-B antibodies
Common MCQ trap Agglutinogens = RBC membrane; Agglutinins = plasma/serum

Exam pearl: Remember: "Agglutinogens are on red cells; agglutinins are in plasma."

Physiology-01.question: ৪২) Maintenance of nearly constant internal environment is called
৪৩) Which blood group has no antibody
Physiology-01.exp:
In the ABO blood group system, individuals with blood group AB have both A and B antigens (agglutinogens) on their RBCs. Therefore, they do not produce anti-A or anti-B antibodies (agglutinins) in their plasma.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Blood group A — Has anti-B antibodies.

  • B. Blood group B — Has anti-A antibodies.

  • D. Blood group O — Has both anti-A and anti-B antibodies.

High-yield Recall

Blood Group RBC Antigen(s) Plasma Antibody(ies)
A A Anti-B
B B Anti-A
AB A and B None
O None Anti-A and Anti-B

Exam pearl

AB blood group has no naturally occurring anti-A or anti-B antibodies, making AB individuals universal recipients for RBC transfusion (AB⁺ if Rh factor is also considered).

Physiology-01.question: ৪৪) Properties of WBC excludes
Physiology-01.exp:
The characteristic properties of white blood cells (WBCs) include:

  • Amoeboid movement

  • Diapedesis (migration through capillary walls)

  • Chemotaxis (movement toward chemical attractants)

  • Phagocytosis (engulfment and destruction of microbes and debris)

Exocytosis is a general cellular process for secretion and is not considered a characteristic property of WBCs in physiology MCQs.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Phagocytosis — A major function of neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages.

  • B. Diapedesis — Enables WBCs to leave blood vessels and enter tissues.

  • C. Chemotaxis — Directs WBCs toward sites of infection or inflammation.

  • D. Exocytosis — A general secretory mechanism, not a defining property of WBCs.

High-yield Recall

Topic Key Point
Amoeboid movement Enables WBC migration
Diapedesis Passage of WBCs through vessel walls
Chemotaxis Movement toward chemical attractants
Phagocytosis Engulfment of pathogens and debris
Major phagocytes Neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages
Common MCQ trap Exocytosis is a cellular process, not a classical property of WBCs

Exam pearl: The four classical properties of WBCs are amoeboid movement, diapedesis, chemotaxis, and phagocytosis.

Physiology-01.question: ৪৫) Blood transfusion is essential in the following conditions except
Physiology-01.exp:
Blood transfusion is indicated when there is a need to increase the oxygen-carrying capacity or replace blood loss, such as in:

  • Severe anemia

  • Acute hemorrhage

  • Major surgery with significant blood loss

In polycythaemia, the patient already has an increased red blood cell mass. Treatment involves phlebotomy (venesection) or cytoreductive therapy—not blood transfusion.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Anemia — Blood transfusion may be required in severe or symptomatic anemia.

  • B. Hemorrhage — Blood transfusion is often essential to replace acute blood loss.

  • D. Surgery — Blood transfusion may be necessary during or after major surgery if there is significant blood loss.

High-yield Recall

Condition Role of Blood Transfusion
Severe anemia Indicated
Acute hemorrhage Indicated
Major surgery with blood loss May be indicated
Polycythaemia Not indicated; treat with phlebotomy
Common MCQ trap Polycythaemia requires blood removal, not blood transfusion

Exam pearl: Polycythaemia is treated by venesection (phlebotomy), whereas anemia and hemorrhage may require blood transfusion.

Physiology-01.question: ৪৬) Stages of hemostasis excludes
Physiology-01.exp:
The stages of haemostasis are the body's responses after vascular injury to stop bleeding. They include:

  1. Vasoconstriction

  2. Platelet plug formation (primary haemostasis)

  3. Coagulation of blood (secondary haemostasis)

Endothelial injury is the trigger for haemostasis, not a stage of the haemostatic process.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • B. Vasoconstriction — First stage of haemostasis; reduces blood flow.

  • C. Platelet plug formation — Second stage; platelets adhere, activate, and aggregate.

  • D. Coagulation of blood — Third stage; fibrin stabilizes the platelet plug.

High-yield Recall

Stage Key Event
Trigger Endothelial (vascular) injury
Stage 1 Vasoconstriction
Stage 2 Platelet plug formation (primary haemostasis)
Stage 3 Coagulation (secondary haemostasis)
Final step Clot retraction and fibrinolysis
Common MCQ trap Endothelial injury initiates haemostasis but is not itself a stage

Exam pearl: Remember: Injury → Vasoconstriction → Platelet plug → Coagulation → Fibrinolysis.

৪৮) Which play an important role in the defense mechanism of the body against the parasites?
Physiology-01.exp:
Eosinophils play a major role in the body's defense against parasitic (especially helminthic) infections. They attach to parasites coated with IgE antibodies and release toxic granule proteins, including:

  • Major basic protein (MBP)

  • Eosinophil cationic protein (ECP)

  • Peroxidase

They are also involved in allergic reactions and help modulate inflammation.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Neutrophil — Primary defense against bacterial infections through phagocytosis.

  • B. Basophil — Releases histamine and heparin; mainly involved in allergic and hypersensitivity reactions.

  • D. Monocyte — Differentiates into macrophages; important for phagocytosis and antigen presentation, but not the primary defense against parasites.

High-yield Recall

Cell Main Function
Neutrophil Bacterial infection, phagocytosis
Eosinophil Parasitic infections, allergic reactions
Basophil Histamine and heparin release, allergy
Monocyte/Macrophage Phagocytosis, antigen presentation
Lymphocyte Adaptive immunity (B and T cells)
Common MCQ trap Eosinophilia is classically associated with parasitic infections and allergic disorders

Exam pearl: Think "Parasites and Allergy = Eosinophils"; "Bacteria = Neutrophils."

Physiology-01.question: ৪৯) RBCs
৫০) Which plays role in Phagocytosis?
Physiology-01.exp:
Monocytes are circulating phagocytic white blood cells. After entering tissues, they differentiate into macrophages, which are highly efficient at:

  • Phagocytosing bacteria, dead cells, and cellular debris

  • Presenting antigens to T lymphocytes

  • Releasing cytokines during inflammation

Although neutrophils are the primary phagocytes in acute bacterial infections, among the given options monocytes are the best answer.

Why the other options are incorrect

  • A. Monocytes — Correct. Differentiate into macrophages, which are professional phagocytes.

  • B. Basophil — Involved in allergic reactions; releases histamine and heparin, not phagocytic.

  • C. Eosinophils — Primarily defend against parasites and participate in allergic reactions; only limited phagocytic activity.

  • D. Monocyte — Duplicate of option A.

High-yield Recall

Cell Main Function
Neutrophil Primary phagocyte in acute bacterial infection
Monocyte/Macrophage Phagocytosis, antigen presentation
Eosinophil Parasitic infections, allergy
Basophil Histamine and heparin release
Common MCQ trap Neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages are the principal phagocytes

Exam pearl: The two major professional phagocytes are neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages; if neutrophils are absent from the options, choose monocytes.
